education.fact: New York City's school system spent $35,796 per pupil in the 2023-24 school year (fiscal 2024), the most among the 100 largest school systems and about double the national average of $17,619. The Census count includes federal, state and city money and employee benefits, but not construction or debt.
education.source: Census Bureau, 2024 Annual Survey of School System Finances

education.fact: Per-pupil current spending in fiscal 2024: New York City $35,796, Los Angeles $25,631, Chicago $24,330, Philadelphia $19,525, Houston $13,950.
The Department of Education spent about $37.7 billion in fiscal 2026 (the figure is not yet final) and had 152,698 staff; it serves nearly one million students in about 1,600 schools.

social_services.fact: An average of 85,066 people a day were in shelters run by the Department of Homeless Services in fiscal 2026, down 2% from the year before but up from 45,563 in fiscal 2022, before asylum seekers began arriving. The count leaves out shelters run by other agencies, such as those for survivors of domestic violence.
566,500 New Yorkers were receiving cash assistance (welfare) in June 2026, 6% fewer than a year earlier, partly because work and job-search requirements resumed.

The city budgets $6.8 billion for Medicaid in fiscal 2027. About $5.4 billion of that is its share of patients' care, which the state froze at the 2015 level; the rest includes extra payments to the city's public hospitals, which the cap does not cover.
social_services.source: State Comptroller, review of the city's financial plan, June 2026

social_services.fact: The city spent $3.75 billion in fiscal 2024 and $3.02 billion in fiscal 2025 on shelter and services for newly arrived migrants, across all agencies; $1.32 billion of the 2025 total was in homeless and social services. That spending is winding down: $1.53 billion so far in fiscal 2026.
social_services.source: State Comptroller, asylum seeker spending report, data through Sept. 30, 2026

social_services.fact: More than a quarter of this line is the city's share of Medicaid, which pays for health care: $6.8 billion of the $23.4 billion budgeted for fiscal 2027.
social_services.source: Office of Management and Budget, adopted budget for fiscal 2027

public_safety.fact: In March 2024 New York City had 32,910 full-time sworn police officers (a Census count that differs slightly from the department's own uniformed headcount), Chicago 11,474, Los Angeles 8,979 and Philadelphia 5,433; against the populations in the same Census file that is about 3.9 officers per 1,000 residents in New York, 4.3 in Chicago, 3.5 in Philadelphia and 2.3 in Los Angeles.
public_safety.source: Census Bureau, 2024 Annual Survey of Public Employment and Payroll

public_safety.fact: The city's jails held an average of 6,954 people a day in fiscal 2026. The Comptroller's last full costing, for fiscal 2021, when the jails held 4,961 people a day, put the cost at $556,539 per person per year, counting costs outside the Department of Correction such as benefits and health care.
public_safety.source: Mayor's Management Report, Fiscal 2026; New York City Comptroller, Dec. 2021

public_safety.fact: The Police Department's uniformed headcount was 34,018 in fiscal 2026, down from 35,910 in fiscal 2020.
public_safety.source: Mayor's Management Report, Fiscal 2026; Comptroller's annual financial report, fiscal 2025

pensions.fact: City pension contributions are budgeted at $8.7 billion in fiscal 2027, down $1 billion from fiscal 2026. A state law let the pension funds re-spread their unfunded liability (the gap between what they hold and what they will owe), lowering the city's payments through fiscal 2032 and raising them from 2033 to 2037; four of the five funds' boards agreed.
pensions.source: New York City Comptroller, comments on the fiscal 2027 adopted budget

pensions.fact: As of June 30, 2025 the five funds held assets covering 92.2% of liabilities for Police, 79.4% for Fire, 87.7% for the New York City Employees' Retirement System, 90.4% for Teachers and 102.6% for the Board of Education system.
361,394 retirees and beneficiaries were drawing city pensions as of June 30, 2024, against 378,991 active members.

benefits.fact: Employee and retiree health insurance is budgeted at $10.9 billion citywide for fiscal 2027, up from $10.6 billion in fiscal 2026; the part for school and City University staff sits in those agencies' budgets, not in this line.
benefits.source: New York City Comptroller, comments on the fiscal 2027 adopted budget

benefits.fact: The retiree health plan covered 288,479 active workers and 260,016 retirees and beneficiaries as of June 30, 2024; its $101.7 billion liability was 5.1 percent funded at June 30, 2025.

The city paid $1.38 billion in judgments and claims in fiscal 2025, against $877 million budgeted at the start of the year. By a different measure, the value of claims settled, fiscal 2024 was the costliest year on record: 13,397 claims for $1.94 billion.
benefits.source: Comptroller's annual financial report, fiscal 2025; New York City Comptroller claims release, April 2025

debt_service.fact: Debt service took 10.2 percent of city tax revenues in fiscal 2025, under the city's 15 percent affordability ceiling, but is projected to reach about 14.2 percent by fiscal 2033.
debt_service.source: New York City Comptroller, annual report on capital debt and obligations, fiscal 2026

debt_service.fact: The city owed $121.0 billion in bonds and notes at the end of fiscal 2025, counting premiums. With leases and other obligations its debt was $133.6 billion, or $15,763 per resident.
debt_service.source: Comptroller's annual financial report, fiscal 2025, ratios of outstanding debt

debt_service.fact: On the measure the Comptroller uses to compare cities, which leaves out most leases, debt per resident in fiscal 2024 was $12,402 in New York City, second highest of the 14 cities compared, after Washington ($21,712); Chicago was $6,659, Los Angeles $5,360, Philadelphia $4,869 and Houston $4,410. The Comptroller cautions that the cities' figures may not be fully comparable.
debt_service.source: New York City Comptroller, annual report on capital debt and obligations, fiscal 2026, Table 19

health.fact: The State Comptroller counts more than $2.4 billion in city support for NYC Health + Hospitals' own operations in fiscal 2025, 145% more than in fiscal 2018. The city also pays the system to run city programs.

Health + Hospitals treated 1,170,529 unique patients in fiscal 2026, 215,554 of them uninsured. Its own spending, projected at $13.2 billion, comes mainly from Medicaid, Medicare and the state's Essential Plan, not the city budget.
The Department of Health and Mental Hygiene spent about $2.84 billion in fiscal 2026 (not yet final).

This line was bigger in fiscal 2025 partly because the city paid Health + Hospitals to run shelters and services for asylum seekers: $874 million in fiscal 2025 by the State Comptroller's count, with nothing budgeted for that in fiscal 2027.
health.source: State Comptroller, asylum seeker spending report; City Council Finance Division, July 2026

general_government.fact: The biggest agency in this line is the Department of Youth and Community Development, which runs after-school programs serving nearly 116,300 participants, the Summer Youth Employment Program, services for runaway and homeless youth and 192 community centers. The city's audited report files it under general government, so this page does too.

The city had 287,422 full-time employees in fiscal 2025, of whom 15,073 were in general government; the fiscal 2027 budget authorizes 307,199 full-time positions, a ceiling that includes unfilled jobs.
general_government.source: Comptroller's annual financial report, fiscal 2025; New York City Comptroller, comments on the fiscal 2027 adopted budget

environmental.fact: Sanitation disposed of 3.13 million tons of refuse in fiscal 2026 and collected 719,000 tons of recycling, a 19.7 percent diversion rate.

Water and sewer bills, not taxes, pay for the water system. The Water Board sets rates to cover the system's costs and the Water Authority's debt, and the Department of Environmental Protection collected over $4.8 billion in fiscal 2026. The Water Board pays the city back for running the system and rents it from the city, $2.4 billion budgeted for fiscal 2027, which the budget counts as city revenue.
environmental.source: Mayor's Management Report, Fiscal 2026; Office of Management and Budget, May 2026

everything_else.fact: The New York City Housing Authority serves 497,649 authorized residents, about 331,700 of them in its 177,565 apartments across 335 developments; the rest hold Section 8 vouchers in private housing. Its own spending, $5.6 billion in fiscal 2026, sits mostly outside the city budget, which gives it $410 million in fiscal 2027 through Housing Preservation and Development.
The Department of Transportation maintains 6,300 miles of streets, 809 bridges and four tunnels, and resurfaced 1,169 lane miles in fiscal 2026.
The three library systems run 220 local library locations, including five research centers.
